author: Carlos Martinez
title: Daytona Road Course on iRacing: Blending the Infield With the Banking
description: My corner-by-corner notes and setup approach for the Daytona Road Course on iRacing, raced from a MOZA R9 direct-drive rig.

sections.p: I run all of this from a fixed-aluminium-extrusion cockpit with a ~MOZA R9 direct drive wheelbase and ~MOZA CRP2 load-cell pedals — no motion, no fancy paint, just a rig built to be honest about what the car is doing. This week it's the Daytona Road Course — one of the tracks I keep coming back to on iRacing, and one where the corner-by-corner details matter more than most. I've raced enough laps here across enough car classes that I've stopped thinking of it as one lap and started thinking of it as a handful of separate problems strung together, which is honestly how I'd recommend approaching any new track once you're past the total-beginner stage.

None of what follows is a substitute for laps. iRacing's tire model and each car's balance shift enough between builds and seasons that exact setup numbers go stale fast — what doesn't go stale is which corners at the Daytona Road Course punish which mistakes, and that's what I'm actually trying to hand off here.

Before I get into setup or technique, it's worth walking the layout once with fresh eyes, because most of the time lost at a new track comes from not knowing what's coming next rather than from any actual driving mistake.

list: The Bus Stop chicane onto the oval — a slow, technical entry into a very different section of track
The oval banking sections — where the car briefly behaves like a superspeedway car before diving back into the infield
The International Horseshoe — a tight, tightening-radius corner that's easy to overslow
The Kink before the tri-oval — deceptively fast for how casual it looks on the map

sections.p: I'd genuinely recommend doing a slow, no-pressure lap or two just looking around before pushing for pace — glance at the runoff, the curbing, and where the track actually widens versus where it only looks like it does. A surprising amount of confidence at the Daytona Road Course comes from simply knowing the track's shape well enough that you're not making decisions on the fly anymore.

sections.h2: Where I set up the car differently here

sections.p: My starting point for the Daytona Road Course is never a totally clean-sheet setup — I take whatever baseline I'm running that week for the car class and adjust from there based on what this specific layout demands.

list: I split the difference between my road-course and oval setups here — the banking wants stability, the infield wants rotation
Ride height comes up slightly for the banked sections so the car doesn't bottom out under the extra loading
I keep the rear anti-roll bar softer than a pure road course to help the car settle after the banking transitions

sections.p: I'd treat all of this as a starting point rather than a final answer. Setup work on iRacing rewards small, deliberate changes tested one at a time far more than it rewards big swings based on a feeling — change one thing, run a handful of laps, and actually compare lap times and how the car felt rather than just going on instinct.

sections.h2: A practice session plan that actually works

olist: Run three or four laps at a moderate pace just to build a mental map of the corners before pushing for time
Push for a genuinely fast lap once the tires and track feel warmed in, and note exactly where you felt like you left time on the table
Adjust one setup parameter based on that feeling, then run another push lap to see if it actually helped
Finish with a longer run at race pace rather than qualifying pace, since that's closer to what you'll actually need on race day

sections.p: The banked sections load the ~MOZA R9 in a way that feels almost like a constant-radius oval corner, then it changes character completely back in the infield — this is a track where FFB settings that feel great in one section can feel wrong in the other, so I compromise rather than chase perfection everywhere.

I mention wheel feel specifically because the Daytona Road Course is a good example of how much a track's character can change what a 'good' FFB setting even means. A profile that feels great somewhere flat and smooth can feel either numb or harsh somewhere with real elevation change or bumps, and this track is one where I've had to actually revisit my base settings rather than assume they'd transfer.

sections.tip: Practice the transition from banking to infield in isolation — it's a small part of the lap but it's where I see the most inconsistent laps from otherwise fast drivers.

sections.h2: Mistakes I still see (and sometimes still make)

list: Treating the banking like a normal corner and turning in too early
Carrying oval-style commitment into the tighter infield sections
Missing the braking point for the International Horseshoe after the speed of the banking

sections.p: What all of these mistakes have in common is that they're habits carried over from somewhere else — a different track, a different car, a different session — rather than something specific to the Daytona Road Course itself. The fix isn't usually a dramatic technique change, it's just deliberately unlearning the habit that doesn't apply here.

sections.h2: Race craft specifically at this track

sections.p: Single-lap pace and race pace at the Daytona Road Course aren't the same skill, and I'd be doing you a disservice if I only talked about qualifying laps. In traffic, the corners that felt straightforward in isolation often play out completely differently — a car ahead braking a fraction earlier than you expected, or a car alongside taking away the line you were planning to use. I try to build in a little more margin at the corners I've flagged above specifically because that's where a first-lap mistake compounds into an actual incident rather than just a slow lap.

None of this replaces seat time — track knowledge on iRacing comes from laps, not from reading about them. But knowing where the trouble spots are before you find them the hard way saves a few incident points along the way. If you're still dialing in your braking feel generally, I wrote up my notes on how Safety Rating actually works separately, and it's worth reading alongside anything track-specific.

faqs.q: What's the hardest corner at the Daytona Road Course on iRacing?
faqs.a: The Bus Stop chicane onto the oval tends to catch the most drivers, based on what I see in replays and incident reports.

faqs.q: Do I need a high-end wheelbase to learn the Daytona Road Course?
faqs.a: No — track knowledge and braking points transfer across wheel setups. A direct drive wheel like my ~MOZA R9 makes the feedback clearer, but it won't teach you the line by itself.

faqs.q: How many laps does it usually take to feel comfortable here?
faqs.a: It varies a lot by driver, but I'd budget a full practice session or two of focused laps before expecting genuine confidence, especially at a technical or blind-corner-heavy track.

faqs.q: Does setup matter more than driving line at this track?
faqs.a: Driving line first, always — a good setup makes a well-driven lap faster, but it won't fix a fundamentally wrong line or braking point.
